This lecithotrophic stage is brief, as the prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The timing of these early life history events under thermal regimes typical of the species' range contrasts sharply with the developmental schedules of more northerly distributed congeners, many of which require a full year or longer to reach reproductive competence. Furthermore, field observations suggest that the onset of first reproduction occurs at approximately 730 days after birth [tR = 730 days after birth], which is considerably later than the attainment of puberty, indicating a delay between sexual maturation and actual spawning in this species.

The combination of early maturation and a compressed adult lifespan places this species firmly on the fast end of the life history continuum, a pattern that is often associated with high annual reproductive effort and elevated juvenile mortality rates. Comparative data from closely related species within the subgenus Catonotus support this interpretation, as all exhibit similar constraints on adult survivorship, and long-term mark-recapture studies in perennial streams have rarely recovered individuals older than 18 months.
